genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: one of the two scientists watches the water that moves below the ground surface
the other scientist follows the watercourses that run in the open
both women study the same resource
water underground cleans itself as it passes through permeable material
surface water carries sediment and plant debris along with it
surface water has to settle before it can be analyzed
the buried reserve sustains the stream when the water runs low
spells of strong flow recharge the buried reserve
text: One of them spends half her working life under the rock, headlamp on, notebook damp in her pocket, tracking water where nobody can see it move. Her colleague works in the open air, boots in the current, walking the channels that lie out in daylight. Both women measure the same water, yet they never meet it in the same state. Below the stone it threads through porous ground and clears itself as it crosses bed after bed of sand. Out in the light it drags silt, leaves and insects along, so a sample has to stand and settle before anyone can test it. The first reads a hidden reserve by how slowly it moves. The second reads a stream by how hard it pushes. Set their records side by side and one thing shows up twice: the buried water feeds the open channel when the level drops, and every strong flow sends water back down to fill the reserve again.

units: the visitor did not expect to enjoy the visit
a first section shows what sand does when the air drives it
a wall crumbles in front of the public behind a glass screen
a second section shows what cold does to water that has seeped in
the rock breaks apart when water freezes inside a crack
a third section deals with chemical attack by plants
two pebbles side by side compare an intact surface with a hollowed one
the fourth section disappoints because it carries too much written text
a rebuilt coastal wall closes the visit
text: Honestly, the show about stone wearing away knocked me sideways, and I had expected nothing from it. First room, the wind one: sand is thrown at a soft slab, and the slab crumbles while you watch, safe behind a pane of glass. Second room, the cold one: water works into a crack, stiffens, swells, and the rock cracks open like a shell. Third room, my favorite, the acid one: quiet mosses gnaw at limestone, and two pebbles lying together make the case, one still smooth, the other bitten full of hollows. Fourth room, the weak one: too much wall text, too little to look at, and you drift off fast. The ending pulls it all back, with a model cliff that the water eats away in front of you, again and again. I walked out thinking nothing hard stays hard, and I went back that same evening, on my own.

units: the writer is writing from a shelter put up beside a basin
the spring stopped flowing with no warning sign
the crew first blamed the measuring instrument
a probe brought up an obstruction made of small stones
workmen pulled the obstruction out by hand
the water came back hard before it settled down
the rock around here breaks up easily under pressure
the blockage happens again with every turn of the season
a metal guard will be fitted upstream
text: I am writing from the hut we put up at the edge of the basin, with the ink half stiff in the pen. Yesterday at first light the spring stopped, no warning of any kind, and the crew blamed the gauge before anything else. Around midday the engineer lowered a probe into the pipe and brought back the answer: gravel, packed tight. Early in the afternoon two workmen cleared the passage by hand, stone after stone, taking their time over it. The flow came back all at once. Water shot up over the rim, then eased into a steady thread. In the evening we pulled the readings together and laid the week out as a curve. The conclusion fits on one line. The rock up here is brittle, it gives way under pressure, and it plugs the pipe every season. A metal grate goes in upstream. I come home once the report is signed.

units: water works into cavities too fine to be seen
freezing makes the water take up more room
that gain in volume widens the crack
the crack stays open once the mild weather returns
mineral deposits and roots move into the opening
the push of growing plants completes the break
the broken rock travels down the slope and is ground into particles
those particles feed the making of a soil
the bare slope and the grassland below share one origin
moving air carries the finest fragments down to the low country
text: What becomes of a stone once water settles in its veins? It learns patience, and then it gives way. The water works into pores so fine that no eye picks them out. Cold arrives, the water stiffens and takes up more room than it should, and the crack widens by a line nobody will ever notice. Mild weather comes back, the water withdraws, and the crack stays open. What follows? Mineral dust drifts in, roots find room to sit, and the push of growing things finishes the work. Should we say the rock dies? No, it scatters. Every splinter goes down the slope, grinds against its own kind, and ends as grains that feed a young soil. The bare ground above and the grassland below are one matter, parted by a long fall. What is finest of all rides the moving air out to the flat country.

units: the filtering unit was clogging far sooner than expected
the readings showed that most of the particles were clay
those particles turn sticky as soon as they meet moisture
the blockage forms in the lower part of the unit
the supervisor proposed a coarse screen set at the inlet
she also proposed a settling tank ahead of the unit
the technician feared a loss of flow at peak demand
two tanks used in turn solved the flow problem
the time between two blockages grew much longer
text: The technician at the basin told the supervisor that the inlet filter was choking up in two weeks instead of six. She asked him whether the load of particles had gone up. He answered that the readings pointed at fine clay, which turns sticky the moment it takes on any moisture and seals the mesh from the bottom. The supervisor put forward a coarse bar screen on the raw water, and then a tank where the water could stand and settle before it reached the filter. The technician pushed back, since a tank of that kind would drag the flow down when demand peaked. She suggested two tanks in parallel, with a switch from one to the other. The trial ran a whole season. The filter now holds eight weeks, and the crew cleans out the tanks instead of buying mesh, which works out a good deal cheaper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the study of rock once rested on the senses of the researcher
the observer judged weight hardness and the sound of a knock
descriptions depended on the memory of whoever had looked
two researchers far apart gave different names to the same material
cutting rock into a transparent slice changed the discipline
that technique makes the crystals and their arrangement visible
the older approach was quick but confused materials that looked alike
the newer approach calls for equipment and patience
the two ways of working are still combined in the field
text: Before optical instruments grew fine enough to be trusted, rock was studied by hand and by eye. The observer weighed a block in the palm, scratched it with a fingernail, listened to the note it gave when struck. A description was worth what the memory of the describer was worth, and two scholars far apart would file the same stone under different names. The thin slice overturned all that. Cut down until the rock lets light through, a sample gives up its crystals, their outlines and the way they sit together, and matter can be named without being touched. The older method read the surface, the newer one questions the structure. One moved fast and was fooled by stones that felt alike. The other asks for a workshop, for patience and for a steady cutting flow. They still work as a pair: on the slope, the hand picks what the slice will confirm.

units: three kinds of soil sit together on one slope
the soil where sand dominates lets water drain away at once
its grains never stick together between the fingers
clay soil holds water and turns sticky in the rain
as it dries clay hardens and splits open
the middle soil keeps the moisture that is useful and drains the surplus
a dark surface layer holds the remains of plants
that layer feeds whatever grows in it
shaping a lump by hand tells you which kind dominates
text: Three kinds of soil share one and the same slope, and the hand tells them apart. Sandy soil lets water drain almost as fast as it arrives. It is open and light, and the grains roll between the fingers without ever clinging. Clay soil does the reverse. It holds on to water, turns sticky under rain, then hardens as it dries until it splits into plates. Loam lies between the two. It keeps back enough moisture for the roots and lets the surplus run off downhill. Above these three sits a dark layer at the surface, thick with the remains of plants, and it feeds everything that grows there. A gardener finds out which soil he has by rolling a damp lump in the palm. It falls apart into dust where sand rules, and it draws out into a smooth rope where clay has the upper hand instead.

units: the group set out before sunrise to watch a spring that flows in bursts

the walk in took nearly an hour along a muddy track
on arrival the site looked like nothing at all
the guide asked the group to wait without making a sound
a deep noise came before the pool drained away
the water rose higher than the tops of the trees
it was over quickly and the visitors were soaked
the guide wrote down the gap between two bursts
text: We set off before sunrise to watch a spring that spills over in bursts, and I grumbled the whole way there, because the cold was already biting my fingers. Our guide, a herder before he gave it up, walked us a solid hour along a track thick with mud. Then we arrived and there was nothing to see: a steaming hole, a warm pool, two birds that could not have cared less. He told us to stand still and make no sound. After a while a low rumble came up out of the ground, the pool drained in one gulp, and the water leapt higher than the tops of the trees, in a warm cloud that soaked us to the socks. It was over fast, and the quiet came back as if nothing had happened. The guide, meanwhile, wrote down the gap between one burst and the last. We walked off wet, laughing, delighted, and I stopped grumbling.

units: take the sample at the depth where the roots grow
leave out the surface layer because it holds debris
dry the sample away from heat so that its structure holds
take out the coarse pieces by passing the material over a screen
keeping them would throw the result off by their weight
then put the material into a jar of water
the particles settle in order from the heaviest down
read the thickness of the layers from the bottom upward
note the color once when wet and once when dry
text: Start by lifting a handful of soil at the depth where the roots run, never from the top, because the upper layer is loaded with debris and will throw your reading off. Spread the sample on paper and let it dry in the shade, since fierce heat bursts the crumbs apart and alters the texture. Sieve the dry material next so the gravel comes out, or its weight will crush the fine fraction in the count. Tip what is left into a jar of clear water, shake it, then put it down and leave it alone. The heavy grains land first and the fine ones after, so the bands can be read through the glass. Measure each band from the bottom upward, because the order of settling tells you what the soil is made of. Write down the color last, wet and dry, since drying turns it into another color altogether.

units: the current has cut into the raised edge down to the roots of the plants

the loose nature of the ground makes it easy to tear away

the path will be moved further from the watercourse
text: On the low side the water has gnawed into the raised edge, right down to the roots of the bushes, and the path that ran along the channel is dropping away in whole sections. The people who live there put it plainly: every rise takes another step off the edge. The ground is loose here, sand mixed with silt, and the current lifts it without effort as it gathers speed in the bend, then carries what it has torn off downstream. The team that looks after the basin ruled out a built wall, costly and blunt, which would only have thrown the force of the water at the far side. They chose to plant the slope with bushes that root and creep, to lay bundles of branches at its foot, and to dig a hollow upstream so the water arrives slower. One season held the toe. The path moves higher, out of reach.
